How the forecast works

For each of 18 destinations and 8 worker types, the model scores the change in annual migrant-worker inflows for a given year against the 2016–2025 average. It adds five terms, each phased in on its own clock:

demand sector trend + workforce shrinkage × ageing sensitivity + building pipeline, phased in over the decade
economy growth outlook × Economic dial, realised by 2030
policy 12 × (national stance + sector carve-out + Political dial), in force by 2027
heat −7 × destination heat × outdoor exposure × Climate dial, rising over time
automation −10 × sector exposure × destination capacity × Automation dial, accelerating
shock 2026 Gulf war losses, fading by 2028–29

Corridor flows multiply each corridor’s base size by its destination’s sector scores and by an origin push: working-age growth, climate exposure (scaled by the Climate dial) and labour-export policy.

Country reports: click any country to zoom into it. Its history is real data: the UN migrant-population series from 1990 to 2024, and World Bank remittances from 2000 to 2025. The forecast lines past today are illustrative. They carry the recent average change forward, scaled by that country’s scenario outlook, with a widening band for uncertainty. In the 3D town, each block’s share of the lots matches its share of migrant jobs. The town grid is a stylised scene: its landmark, building colours and vehicles evoke the named city. The land around it is real. Elevation comes from AWS Terrain Tiles[81], and coastlines, lakes, rivers, built-up areas, peaks and place names from Natural Earth[82]. Heights are exaggerated (the factor is shown under the compass), and distances beyond the town are compressed so that distant landforms such as Mount Fuji or the Himalaya stay in view. Bearings are true. Coastal cities get a port, river cities a bridge, and inland cities a coach station and airfield. Sound is generated in the browser. Footsteps, traffic, work sites and the water get louder as you move the camera closer to them. Cranes mark job types that are growing and barriers mark those that are shrinking.

Protection gap: for each destination and worker type, the model scores the rules a migrant worker meets on paper, from 0 (strongest) to 1. It adds four parts: 0.35 × employer tie (free to change 0, conditional ½, needs consent 1, plus a quarter where an exit visa is still required); 0.20 × recruitment fees (banned 0, regulated or capped ½, allowed 1); 0.15 × the share of five ILO conventions not ratified (C189, C097, C143, C181 and the 2014 forced-labour protocol); and 0.30 × a work-specific rule. For domestic work that is labour-law coverage. For outdoor work it is the heat rule, scaled by the destination’s heat and the Climate dial. The rules are sourced and dated. The weights are this model’s judgement: the employer tie weighs most because the ILO’s forced-labour indicators centre on a worker’s ability to leave. The index does not measure enforcement. The watchlist multiplies it by yearly arrivals through the modelled corridors.

Sourced: migrant stock, working-age projections (UN WPP 2024, computed for all 45 countries), remittances, policy measures and their dates, corridor sizes marked as verified, sector and climate evidence.

Model assumptions: policy stance scores (−2 to +2, from a September 2026 policy review), economic outlook, heat, automation capacity, sector mixes, and the size of unverified corridors. The dossier marks estimated corridors.

Limits:

  • Irregular migration, refugees and internal migration are outside the model.
  • Gulf working-age projections already assume future migration, so they are not used as a demand signal there.
  • Policy can change faster than any model. Re-check the measures before quoting them.

Sources
